title: Benefit of switching to firmonertinib following almonertinib-induced interstitial pneumonitis in a patient with advanced non-small-cell lung cancer: a case report
author: Lingying Wang; Pan Yang; Hu Luo
text:
Abstract
Almonertinib, a representative epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor (EGFR-TKI), is the first-line standard treatment for EGFR-mutant advanced non-small-cell lung cancer; however, it may induce drug-related interstitial lung disease (ILD). This case report presents a 67-year-old female with advanced lung adenocarcinoma, who was diagnosed with an EGFR exon 19 deletion mutation. After 2 months of first-line almonertinib treatment (110 mg/day), a PR was achieved; however, progressive respiratory distress emerged. Chest computed tomography revealed ground-glass opacities accompanied by grid-like changes in both lungs, leading to a diagnosis of EGFR-TKI-related ILD (grade 2). Following glucocorticoid treatment and medication discontinuation, the lung lesions improved. Given the persistent tumor activity, the patient was switched to firmonertinib (80 mg/day) for targeted therapy. This switch did not lead to a recurrence of ILD symptoms, with a progression-free survival exceeding 5 months and good tolerability. This suggests that for patients with ILD associated with almonertinib and firmonertinib may serve as an effective and safe alternative. Closely monitoring ILD in clinical practice and promptly switching to similar drugs may avoid chemotherapy intervention and optimize treatment strategies. This case marks the first report of clinical experience achieving sustained remission by switching to a similar drug, firmonertinib, in patients with ILD related to almonertinib.
Keywords: almonertinib, EGFR exon 19 deletion mutation, firmonertinib, interstitial lung disease
Case introduction
A 67-year-old Asian female presented to our department on 26 June 2024 with a chief complaint of right-sided chest pain. 18F-flurodeoxyglucose PET/computed tomography (CT) imaging revealed the following findings: (a) A spiculated mass measuring 33 × 27 mm in the apical segment of the right upper lobe, demonstrating ill-defined pleural contact and increased metabolic activity; (b) metabolically active bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, suspicious for metastatic involvement; (c) nodular pleural thickening with focal hypermetabolism along the right hemithorax; (d) subpleural micronodules in both lungs without significant FDG avidity; (e) minimal right pleural effusion (Figs. 1 and 2a–d). CT-guided core needle biopsy of the right upper lobe lesion confirmed lung adenocarcinoma with the following immunopurified: TTF-1(+), P40(−), CK7(+), Ki-67(40%+), anaplastic lymphoma kinase fusion-negative by immunohistochemistry (D5F3). Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) exon 19 deletion was detected using amplification refractory mutation system PCR (AmoyDx Mutations Detection Kit, AmoyDx, Xiamen, China). Tumor proportion score for programmed cell death ligand 1 (22C3 pharmDx) was less than 1%. The final diagnosis was stage IVA (union for International Cancer Control 8th edition) lung adenocarcinoma with pleuropulmonary and lymph node metastases (cT2N3M1a IVA, EGFR 19del). First-line therapy with almonertinib 110 mg orally once daily was initiated on 20 July 2024.
Two months after initiating almonertinib therapy, the patient developed a persistent dry cough with scant sputum production accompanied by progressive exertional dyspnea. High-resolution CT (HRCT) on 8 October 2024 demonstrated partial response (PR) of the right upper lobe mass (reduced from 33 × 27 to 15 × 10 mm) alongside newly emerged diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities, with stable mediastinal lymphadenopathy and persistent right pleural thickening (Fig. 2e–h). Laboratory findings revealed leukocytosis (white blood cell: 13.27 × 109/L; neutrophils: 84.9%) and elevated inflammatory markers (erythrocyte sedimentation rate: 44 mm/h, interleukin-6: 16.7 pg/ml), though infectious workup including serum biomarkers (procalcitonin 0.03 ng/ml; β-D-glucan < 20 pg/ml), microbiological cultures, and fungal antigen testing returned negative. Given the temporal association with EGFR-tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) exposure and characteristic HRCT patterns, drug-induced interstitial lung disease (ILD, CTCAE grade 2) was prioritized over infectious etiologies. Immediate almonertinib discontinuation combined with intravenous methylprednisolone (40 mg/day) yielded rapid symptom resolution within 48 h, followed by a structured steroid taper from oral prednisone 50 mg/day (18 October) to 20 mg/day (13 December) with concomitant radiologic improvement. Notably, 29 October surveillance CT revealed paradoxical enlargement of the primary lesion, prompting switch to firmonertinib 80 mg daily. Subsequent imaging confirmed secondary PR per RECIST v1.1 (Fig. 2m), achieving progression-free survival exceeding 5 months with favorable tolerability (eastern cooperative oncology group (ECOG) performance status 0 maintained throughout). And serial HRCT documented sustained resolution of ILD features during steroid tapering, establishing a causal relationship with almonertinib toxicity. Glucocorticoids were discontinued on 30 December, with no subsequent recurrence of interstitial pneumonia clinically or radiographically.
Discussion
Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC), accounting for 85% of lung malignancies, demonstrates a high prevalence of EGFR mutations in Asian populations, with a 50.2% mutation rate in adenocarcinomas [1,2]. Third-generation EGFR-TKIs, including osimertinib, firmonertinib, and almonertinib have become first-line therapeutic mainstays for EGFR-mutant NSCLC through optimized kinase domain targeting. While these agents exhibit improved central nervous system penetration and T790M resistance mutation coverage, their safety profiles diverge significantly in drug-induced ILD incidence: 3.7% for osimertinib [3], 0.9% for almonertinib [4], and 0.56% for firmonertinib [1]. ILD risk stratification models identify male gender, smoking history (>30 pack-years), pre-existing pulmonary comorbidities (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease/emphysema), recent radiotherapy, and suboptimal performance status (ECOG ≥ 2) as key predisposing factors [5].
This case illustrates three critical clinical dilemmas: (a) Timing of ILD onset: the patient developed CTCAE grade 2 pneumonitis at 2 months of almonertinib therapy, preceding the typical 3–6 month risk window, suggesting accelerated immunopathogenesis in EGFR 19Del carriers. (b) Therapeutic paradox: steroid-induced tumor flare (25% lesion enlargement post-TKI cessation) versus sustained oncologic control requirement. (c) TKI rechallenge strategy: balancing ILD recurrence risk against EGFR pathway dependency. Our management protocol – immediate TKI discontinuation, high-dose methylprednisolone (0.5 mg/kg/day), and structured steroid taper – achieved radiologic ILD resolution within 4 weeks. Notably, the subsequent transition to firmonertinib under steroid coverage yielded dual benefits: secondary PR (RECIST v1.1) and absence of ILD recurrence over 5-month follow-up.
Emerging evidence supports selective TKI rechallenge post-ILD. A Japanese multicenter study (n = 5) demonstrated that resuming EGFR-TKIs with concurrent prednisolone (0.5 mg/kg) significantly prolonged median overall survival versus permanent discontinuation (15.5 versus 3.5 months; P = 0.029) [6]. Mechanistically, firmonertinib’s trifluoromethoxypyridine moiety enhances mutant EGFR selectivity while minimizing wild-type EGFR off-target effects – a pharmacokinetic advantage corroborated by its sixfold lower ILD incidence compared with osimertinib [7]. This structural optimization may explain our patient’s sustained response without pneumonitis recurrence.
In summary, despite the low incidence of ILD caused by EGFR-TKI, the disease progresses rapidly and carries a high mortality rate. Early detection and timely treatment are crucial. This case serves as a reminder: (a) patients undergoing EGFR-TKI treatment should be screened to avoid those at high risk. (b) Patients on EGFR-TKI therapy need regular check-ups for lung function and chest CT scans to promptly identify early signs of ILD. If a patient experiences sudden worsening of cough or shortness of breath, prompt chest CT evaluation is essential. (c) Patients with grade 3 or higher ILD should discontinue the medication immediately and undergo hormone therapy. Once the interstitial lung changes are under control, switching to a less ILD-prone EGFR-TKI may offer benefits to those who have previously experienced ILD.
